393.title: Listening for the ripe
393.hook: the Anand invites us to hear what is true beneath the noise
393.howItsDone: In the gurdwara the sangat largely listens: to kirtan, to the reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and to the day's hukamnama, which Sikhs hear as guidance for that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kachee, and your line, ripe words. Did you let one sentence wait a breath before you said it? Yesterday was the speaker's side. Today, the listener's. Day three hundred ninety-three.

A wedding hall, ten minutes before the food. Two hundred people talking at once, a toddler shrieking, someone testing a microphone. And across the room, through all of it, somebody says your name, and your head turns. Psychologists call it the cocktail party effect: the ear can pull one voice out of a roar when it's tuned for it. Yesterday the Anand said the hearers of unripe words are unripe too. Which raises the question: what is the ear tuned for? Today: suniai.
screen: `A LOUD HALL. SOMEONE SAYS YOUR NAME.` → `THE EAR PULLS ONE VOICE FROM A ROAR.` → `WHAT IS YOUR EAR TUNED FOR?`

segments.voice: Pauri twenty-four's line runs, in paraphrase: unripe are those who speak, unripe are those who hear. Guru Amar Das doesn't let the listener off the hook. A ripe word can fall on an ear that's somewhere else, and then it's as if it was never said. But the Sikh answer to that isn't to listen less. It's to listen better. Look at what happens in a gurdwara. The ragis sing the kirtan, and the sangat listens. The Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud, and the room listens. Each day a hukamnama, the order, is read from wherever the Guru Granth Sahib opens, and Sikhs hear it as guidance for that day. Hearing sits near the center of it all. Guru Nanak had already said this in the Japji. Four pauris in a row, eight through eleven, keep beginning their lines with one word, suniai: by listening. By listening, they say in paraphrase, sorrow and wrongdoing are wiped away; by listening, even an ordinary person comes to know truth and contentment. So the Anand's warning and the Japji's praise fit together. The ear can be unripe, filled with the noise of maya, gossip, the scroll. Or it can be tuned, the way it's tuned for your name in a crowded hall, so that one true sentence comes through. Hear the true.
screen: `PAURI 24: THE HEARERS CAN BE UNRIPE TOO.` · `IN THE GURDWARA, HEARING IS THE MAIN ACT.` · `JAPJI 8–11: SUNIAI, BY LISTENING.` · `TUNE THE EAR LIKE IT'S TUNED FOR YOUR NAME.` · then, large: `HEAR THE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Close your eyes and let the sounds come in: traffic, a fridge, a voice in another room, your own breath. Don't name them or chase them. Just let the ear be wide. Then, inside all that, listen for one thing that's simply true right now. My breath is moving. The light is on. Someone I love is alive. Let that one sentence come through the noise, the way your name does. If you pray, you can listen to Waheguru said once, silently, inside. The bell holds the time.
Suniai, by listening. The Anand warns that hearers can be unripe; the Japji says that by suniai, sorrow is wiped away. Tune the ear for what is true.
Your line: hear the true. Today, in one conversation, listen for a single sentence that's honest and real, and let the rest go by. Day three hundred ninety-three.

pairs: the hearers can be unripe too

options: a fortune that predicts their day.
the hukamnama: the day's order, guidance to hear.
a test of how well they know the text.
fork.reveal: it's called the hukamnama, the order, and Sikhs hear it as guidance for that day.

trapdoor: what you thought: listening for the ripe means tuning out everyone you disagree with.
what it means: tuning the ear for what is true under the noise, since the Anand warns that hearers too can be unripe.

394.title: O my body
394.hook: the Guru speaks to the body: what have you done since you came into the world (Anand, the body pauris)
394.howItsDone: These pauris are part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib, which many Sikhs recite each morning; the Sikh householder way lives faith out in the body, through work, family and service such as langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suniai, and your line, hear the true. Did one honest sentence come through the noise? Today the Anand stops talking about us and starts talking to us, part by part. Day three hundred ninety-four.

Halfway up a long flight of stairs, a man stops, puts a hand on his knee, and says out loud: come on, you can do this. People talk to their bodies all the time. We scold a stiff back, plead with a stomach before a big meeting, thank our legs at the end of a race. Usually it's a joke, or a complaint. Near the end of the Anand, Guru Amar Das does it too, on purpose, and the question he asks is not a joke. Today: sareeraa.
screen: `A MAN ON THE STAIRS: COME ON, KNEE.` → `WE ALL TALK TO OUR BODIES.` → `THE ANAND DOES IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Toward the close of the Anand comes a run of pauris that speak directly to parts of a person. The first begins ae sareeraa mairiaa: O my body. And then a question, in paraphrase: since you came into this world, what have you done? What deeds have you done, body, since you arrived? It sounds like an accusation, and it partly is. The pauri goes on: the One who fashioned you, you never kept in your mind. But it doesn't stop there. By the Guru's grace, it says, the Lord comes to dwell in the mind, and Guru Amar Das ends with a promise: the body that fixes its attention on the True Guru is accepted, approved, parvaan. So the question isn't a verdict. It's a mirror held up halfway through a life, with a way forward written underneath. Notice who is being asked. Not the soul, not the mind. The body. This pauri doesn't treat the body as a cage to escape. Elsewhere Guru Amar Das calls the body the Lord's temple, and Sikh life is lived in the body, as a householder: working, cooking, raising children, serving in langar with your own two hands. Uncut hair, kept as part of the Khalsa discipline, is explained by some as keeping the body as it was given. So the body isn't the problem in this pauri. It's the one being invited. Hands, feet, a whole lifetime of days: what will they be used for? O my body.
screen: `AE SAREERAA MAIRIAA: O MY BODY.` · `WHAT HAVE YOU DONE SINCE YOU CAME?` · `BY GRACE, THE BODY IS ACCEPTED.` · `NOT A CAGE: THE ONE BEING INVITED.` · then, large: `O MY BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your body for one thing. Sit comfortably and let your attention move slowly from your feet up to your head. Somewhere along the way, stop at one part that did something for you today. The hands that made breakfast. The legs that carried you to the bus. The lungs, still going. Rest your attention there, and quietly say thank you to it, the way you'd thank a friend who helped you move house. Then breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let it settle into that place. The bell holds the time.
Sareeraa, O body. Ae sareeraa mairiaa: the Anand asks the body what it has done in this world, and promises that the body turned toward the True Guru is accepted.
Your line: what have you done. Today, when you use your hands for something ordinary, washing a cup, carrying a bag, ask them quietly what they're doing it for. Day three hundred ninety-four.

screen: `DAY 394 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LIGHT PLACED IN YOU.`

what it means: the body is asked what its days are for, and promised acceptance when it turns toward the True Guru.

395.title: The light placed in you
395.hook: the body came into the world when the Lord placed His light within it (Anand, the body pauris)
395.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib each morning, and the teaching that the one divine light, jot, dwells in every body is often given as a reason Sikhs reject caste and serve all in langar alike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sareeraa, the Anand asking the body what it has done in this world. What have you done? Did you thank one part of yourself? Today the next pauri speaks to the body again, and tells it where it came from. Day three hundred ninety-five.

A dim room, a gray screen, two parents holding hands. The technician moves the wand and points: there. A tiny flicker, fast as a bird's wing. Many parents say that moment changed something; before it there was news, and after it there was someone. Nobody in the room could tell you exactly what had arrived. The Anand has an answer, and it's the next thing Guru Amar Das says to the body. Today: jot.
screen: `A SCREEN, A FLICKER, TWO PARENTS.` → `BEFORE: NEWS. AFTER: SOMEONE.` → `WHAT ARRIVED?`

segments.voice: The pauri starts the same way as yesterday's, ae sareeraa mairiaa, sareeraa. But this time it doesn't ask what the body has done. It tells the body something. In paraphrase: the Lord placed His light within you, and then you came into the world. And it says it twice, turning the line around, as if to make sure it's heard. The Gurmukhi word is jot, light, the same word Sikhs use when they say the one light passed from Guru Nanak to each Guru after him. Here that light is placed in every body. Notice the order. First the light, then the arrival. The body doesn't earn the light later by being good; it comes into the world because the light is already in it. The pauri goes on: the Lord is Himself mother and Himself father, the One who made living beings and showed them the world. And by the Guru's grace, someone understands, and then the whole world is seen as a play, chalat, the Lord's own wonderful display. It closes with Guru Amar Das's signature line: the One who made the root of creation placed His light in you, and then you came into the world. Yesterday's question was hard: what have you done? Today's line is the ground under it. Whatever the body has or hasn't done, the light was placed there first. Many Sikhs hear this as the reason no one can be looked down on. Every body in the room arrived the same way. Light in the body.
screen: `O MY BODY, AGAIN: NOT A QUESTION NOW.` · `JOT: THE LORD'S LIGHT, PLACED IN YOU.` · `FIRST THE LIGHT, THEN THE ARRIVAL.` · `MOTHER AND FATHER, AND THE WORLD A PLAY.` · then, large: `LIGHT IN THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel your pulse. Lay two fingers lightly on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb, or at the side of your neck under the jaw. Wait until you find it. Don't count. Just feel it arrive, again and again, without being asked. You didn't start it and you aren't running it. Let that be enough for a while. If the Anand's line helps, let it ride along with the beat: light in the body. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, softly. The bell holds the time.
Jot, light. In the Anand, the Lord places His jot in the body, and only then does the body come into the world.
Your line: light in the body. Today, feel your pulse once more, maybe in a queue or before you sleep, and remember what the pauri says came first. Day three hundred ninety-five.

396.title: O my eyes
396.hook: the eyes are told the Lord put His light in them, so see Him in all (Anand, the eyes)
396.howItsDone: This pauri is part of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning; seeing the one light in everyone is often given as the ground of Sikh equality, lived out in sangat and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jot, and your line, light in the body. Did you feel your pulse and remember what came first? Today the Anand turns from the whole body to two small parts of it. Day three hundred ninety-six.

There's a kind of video people love to share: a child getting her first pair of glasses. She puts them on in the optician's chair, looks up at her mother, and her face changes. Then she looks out the window, and points. Leaves. She hadn't known trees had separate leaves. Nothing outside had changed. Her sight had. The Anand has a pauri like that moment, spoken straight to the eyes. Today: naetr.
screen: `A CHILD'S FIRST GLASSES.` → `TREES HAVE SEPARATE LEAVES.` → `THE WORLD THE SAME, THE SIGHT NEW.`

segments.voice: After the body, Guru Amar Das speaks to the eyes: ae naetrahu mairiho, O my eyes. In paraphrase: the Lord has put His light in you, so look on no one but the Lord. That could sound like a command to stop seeing the world. Read on, and it means nearly the opposite. The next lines say: this whole world you see is the Lord's own form; the Lord's form is what comes into view. So the eyes aren't told to look away from people and places. They're told what they're actually looking at. Then the turn, and it's honest. By the Guru's grace, Guru Amar Das says, I understood: wherever I look, the Lord is one, and there's no other. And the closing line: these eyes were blind, and meeting the True Guru, they received divine sight. The phrase is dib drisat, a sight that sees more than surfaces. Like the child in the glasses, the world hasn't changed. The eyes have. Notice the link to yesterday. Yesterday the light was placed in the body. Today the same light is in the eyes, and with that light they're meant to find the same light in everything they see. Light looking at light. Sikh teachers draw from this a reason the way you look at someone matters: at the stranger on the bus, the person serving you, the one you find hard. The pauri doesn't ask the eyes to close. It asks them to see Him.
screen: `AE NAETRAHU MAIRIHO: O MY EYES.` · `THIS WORLD YOU SEE IS THE LORD'S FORM.` · `THESE EYES WERE BLIND, NOW DIVINE SIGHT.` · `LIGHT LOOKING AT LIGHT.` · then, large: `EYES, SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one person as light. Bring to mind someone you'll see today, maybe someone ordinary, maybe someone difficult. Picture their face clearly: the way they stand, the look they get when they're tired. Then hold the Anand's line next to the picture. The same light placed in you was placed in them. Don't force a feeling. Just let the picture and the line sit side by side, and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, with that face in mind. The bell holds the time.
Naetr, eye. Ae naetrahu mairiho: the Anand tells the eyes the Lord's light is in them, that the world they see is His form, and that meeting the True Guru gives divine sight.
Your line: eyes, see him. Today, when you look at the person you pictured, look one second longer than usual, and remember what the pauri says is there. Day three hundred ninety-six.

397.title: O my ears
397.hook: the ears were sent to hear the truth (Anand, the ears)
397.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite the full Anand Sahib each morning, and many keep kirtan or recorded gurbani playing at home, at work or while driving, so the ears are filled with the Guru's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naetr, and your line, eyes, see him. Did you look at someone one second longer than usual? Today, the next address in the Anand: from the eyes to the ears. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

Here's a small fact about your head. Your eyes have lids. Your ears don't. You can shut out a sight in a blink, but you can't close your ears against a car alarm, a neighbor's argument, or a song you hate. They're on duty all night, which is why an alarm clock works. Whatever is said near you goes in, wanted or not. So it matters a great deal what the ears are for. The Anand gives them a job description. Today: sravan.
screen: `EYES HAVE LIDS. EARS DON'T.` → `ON DUTY ALL NIGHT.` → `SO WHAT ARE THE EARS FOR?`

segments.voice: After the body and the eyes, Guru Amar Das turns to the ears: ae sravanahu mairiho, O my ears. And he says, in paraphrase: you were sent to hear the Truth. Sent. The word is pathaae, sent, the way a messenger is sent. The ears aren't just holes in the head that catch whatever passes. They were sent here with a purpose. The pauri goes on: joined to this body, listen to the true bani. And it says what happens when they do. Hearing it, mind and body become hariaa, green, the way a field in Punjab turns green after the rains, and the tongue is absorbed in its sweetness. Then the pauri admits the limit: the True One is unseen and wondrous, and His state cannot be put into words. The ears can hear the Word; they can't hear around it to the whole. It closes: hear the ambrosial Name and be made pure; you were sent to hear the Truth. A few days ago the Anand warned that hearers can be unripe. This pauri is the other side of that coin. The same ears that soak up gossip in the break room were sent for something else. They can't close, so the pauri gives them something true to hear instead. Ears, hear truth.
screen: `AE SRAVANAHU MAIRIHO: O MY EARS.` · `PATHAAE: SENT, LIKE A MESSENGER.` · `HEARING THE TRUE BANI, LIFE TURNS GREEN.` · `NO LIDS, SO GIVE THEM SOMETHING TRUE.` · then, large: `EARS, HEAR TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to one true thing. Cup your palms gently over your ears for a few breaths and notice the low hush that's left. Then lift your hands and let the world back in. Now choose what the ears will hold: a minute of kirtan or gurbani played softly, if you have one, or one plain sound that is simply there, like your own breath. No judging, no planning a reply. Just hearing. If you pray, you can hear Waheguru once, inside. The bell holds the time.
Sravan, ear. Ae sravanahu mairiho: the Anand tells the ears they were sent to hear the Truth, and that hearing the true bani turns mind and body green.
Your line: ears, hear truth. Today, choose one stretch of time, a commute, a meal, the dishes, and decide on purpose what your ears will hear. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 397 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CAVE AND THE BREATH.`

398.title: The cave and the breath
398.hook: the Lord set the soul in the cave of the body and played the breath like music (Anand)
398.howItsDone: This pauri is part of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning; in the gurdwara, kirtan is commonly sung to the harmonium and tabla, and many Sikhs pair simran, remembering the Name, with the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sravan, and your line, ears, hear truth. Did you choose what your ears would hear for a while? Body, eyes, ears: today the Anand looks at the whole body again, from inside. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

During kirtan, watch the ragi's left hand. While the right hand plays the keys of the harmonium, the left hand works the bellows at the back, folding and unfolding, steady, the whole time. Without that push of air, the keys are just wood. With it, the hall fills with sound. Today's pauri is far older than the harmonium. But it sees the same idea, inside every person. Today: gufaa.
screen: `THE RAGI'S LEFT HAND ON THE BELLOWS.` → `NO AIR, NO MUSIC.` → `THE SAME IDEA, INSIDE A PERSON.`

segments.voice: The pauri opens, in paraphrase: the beloved Lord placed the soul inside the cave, and played the instrument of the breath. The cave, gufaa, is the body: dark, enclosed, hollow, like the caves where people in India have long gone to meditate. The instrument, vaajaa, is played by pavan, air, breath. So every breath is the Lord playing music in a cave. Then the pauri gets more specific. In that body, it says, nine doors were made plain to see, and the tenth was kept hidden. The pauri doesn't list the nine; commentators read them as the body's openings: the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the mouth and the two below. The tenth door, dasvaa duaar, is hidden. Sikh teachers describe it in different ways; one common reading is an inner opening, not a physical one, the place where a person comes to know the One. And the pauri says how it's found: through the Guru's door, with loving faith, some are shown the tenth door. There, it says, are many forms, the Name, the nine treasures, and no one can find the end of them. It closes by repeating its first line: the Lord placed the soul in the cave and played the breath. Notice the order of this week's pauris. The body was asked what it had done, told where its light came from, then the eyes and ears were given their work. Now, underneath all of it, the breath: the music nobody has to remember to play. Breath is music.
screen: `GUFAA: THE BODY AS A CAVE.` · `PAVAN: BREATH PLAYS THE INSTRUMENT.` · `NINE DOORS PLAIN, THE TENTH HIDDEN.` · `THE GURU'S DOOR SHOWS THE TENTH.` · then, large: `BREATH IS MUSIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe and hear it. Sit still, and let the room go quiet around you. Breathe in through the nose, a little slower than usual, and listen to the sound it makes. Breathe out and listen to that sound too. In, out, like the ragi's hand on the bellows. Don't try to make it beautiful. It already is music, the pauri says. Just keep hearing it. If you pray, you can let Waheguru ride along on one breath. The bell holds the time.
Gufaa, cave. In the Anand, the Lord places the soul in the gufaa of the body and plays the breath like an instrument; nine doors are open, and the tenth is hidden.
Your line: breath is music. Today, at one moment of hurry, stop and hear three breaths go in and out, like bellows. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

399.title: Grace gives the Word
399.hook: the Word comes by grace, and with it the bliss (Anand)
399.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of grace as nadar, kirpa or gur prasaad, and the phrase gur prasaad closes the Mool Mantar that opens the Guru Granth Sahib; many Sikhs begin and end their daily prayers by asking for the Guru's grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gufaa, and your line, breath is music. Did you stop for three breaths in a hurry? Today, a thread that runs under every pauri we've heard this week. Day three hundred ninety-nine.

You reach the front of the line at a coffee counter and the barista says: it's paid for. The person ahead of you covered it and left. No name, no way to pay them back. For some, the first feeling is a small awkwardness. People are used to earning things, trading, keeping the account even. A gift with no way to return it is strangely hard to hold. The Anand says the most important thing a person can receive arrives exactly like that. Today: gur prasaad.
screen: `IT'S PAID FOR. NO NAME.` → `WE'RE USED TO KEEPING ACCOUNTS EVEN.` → `THE ANAND: IT ARRIVES LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: Listen back over this week's pauris and one phrase keeps returning: gur parsaadee, by the Guru's grace. The body pauri said that by the Guru's grace the Lord comes to dwell in the mind. The light pauri said that by the Guru's grace a person understands. The eyes pauri said: by the Guru's grace I understood that the Lord is one. Again and again, when a pauri reaches its turning point, it doesn't say by effort, or by cleverness, or by study. It says grace. And earlier, it said the same in other words: the gift is given to the one the Lord blesses. The phrase is there on the first page too. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, ends on it: gur prasaad, known by the Guru's grace. Gurbani uses several words for grace. Nadar is a glance, the look of the Lord resting on someone. Kirpa is mercy. Karam, in gurbani, can mean grace, a gift freely given. Notice that the grace here comes through the Guru: gur parsaadee, not a lucky break. So what does grace give? In the Anand, it gives the Word, the Guru's shabad, and with the Word comes anand, bliss. That doesn't make effort pointless; Sikh life is full of discipline, work and service. It changes what the effort is for. You don't buy the gift. You keep the door open, and say thank you. Grace gives.
screen: `GUR PARSAADEE: BY THE GURU'S GRACE.` · `IT RETURNS AT EVERY TURNING POINT.` · `NADAR, KIRPA, KARAM: WORDS FOR GRACE.` · `GRACE GIVES THE WORD; THE WORD, BLISS.` · then, large: `GRACE GIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive one gift without earning it. Notice what is being given to you right now, this minute, with no bill attached. The floor holding you up. Air arriving at every breath. Light to see by. Pick one. Don't calculate whether you deserved it, and don't plan how to repay it. Just receive it, the way you'd take a warm cup somebody handed you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, as thanks. The bell holds the time.
Gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace. This week in the Anand: ripe words, ears tuned for the true, the body, the light, the eyes, the ears, the breath, and under all of it, gur prasaad.
Your line: grace gives. Today, pass one small gift on, unasked and unsigned, the way the stranger at the counter did. Day three hundred ninety-nine.

original.note: Gurmukhi: gur prasaad, by the Guru's grace; the last words of the Mool Mantar.

trapdoor: what you thought: grace is a reward for being good enough.
what it means: the Word is a gift freely given; with it comes bliss, and effort keeps the door open rather than buying it.
what a scholar hears: gurbani has a cluster of grace words, nadar, kirpa, prasaad, and karam, where the Persian sense of karam as generosity sits beside the Indic sense of deeds.
